{{Hatnote|For the 1995&ndash;2001 printed game period, see [[Decipher era]].}}
'''Decipher, Inc.''' (often just '''Decipher''') was the Norfolk, Virginia game company that published the printed ''Star Wars'' Customizable Card Game (SWCCG) from December 1995 through 2001.<ref name="wp-decipher">[https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decipher,_Inc. Decipher, Inc.], Wikipedia</ref><ref name="wp-swccg">[https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star_Wars_Customizable_Card_Game Star Wars Customizable Card Game], Wikipedia</ref>

[[File:Decipher logo 1999.jpg|thumb|right|220px|Decipher logo, 1999. Source: LOTR-TCG wiki.]]

== Founder / leadership ==

[[Warren Holland]] founded Decipher in '''1983''' and was its Chairman and CEO. The company was headquartered in downtown Norfolk, Virginia.<ref name="ia-about">[https://web.archive.org/web/20000815233727/http://www.decipher.com/aboutdecipher/index.html About Decipher], Decipher.com (Internet Archive, 15 August 2000)</ref><ref name="ia-findus">[https://web.archive.org/web/20000815233727/http://www.decipher.com/aboutdecipher/findus/ Find Us], Decipher.com (Internet Archive, 15 August 2000)</ref><ref name="wp-decipher" />

== Early years (puzzles and party games) ==

Decipher began in 1983 with contest jigsaw puzzles. It then built a long-running party-game line around ''How to Host a Murder'', and later marketed ''Pente'' under a license acquired from Parker Brothers.<ref name="wp-decipher" /><ref name="ia-vision">[https://web.archive.org/web/20000815233727/http://www.decipher.com/aboutdecipher/vision/ Vision], Decipher.com (Internet Archive, 15 August 2000) — company statement signed Warren Holland, Chairman and CEO, citing inception in 1983</ref> The company's slogan of the CCG era was '''Decipher: The Art of Great Games'''.<ref name="wook-decipher">[https://starwars.fandom.com/wiki/Decipher Decipher], Wookieepedia</ref><ref name="lotr-decipher">[https://wiki.lotrtcgpc.net/wiki/Decipher Decipher], LOTR-TCG Wiki</ref>

== CCG era (overview) ==

After ''Magic: The Gathering'' popularized collectible card games, designers [[Tom Braunlich]] and [[Rollie Tesh]] pitched a media-licensed CCG approach. Decipher's first major CCG was the [[Star Trek CCG|''Star Trek: The Next Generation'' CCG]] (1994), followed by SWCCG (1995). Later titles included ''Austin Powers'', ''Young Jedi'', ''Jedi Knights'', ''The Lord of the Rings'' TCG, several youth-market licenses (''.hack'', ''Beyblade'', ''Mega Man''), the original-IP ''WARS'' TCG, and finally ''Fight Klub''.<ref name="wp-decipher" /><ref name="lotr-decipher" /> At peak, Star Wars CCG sales were among the top non-''Magic'' CCGs.<ref name="lotr-decipher" /><ref name="wp-decipher" />

== SWCCG ==

Decipher released SWCCG under a Lucasfilm license.<ref name="wp-decipher" /> Its designers were [[Tom Braunlich]], [[Rollie Tesh]], [[Jerry Darcy]] and [[Warren Holland]] (see [[Creators of SWCCG]]).<ref name="wp-swccg" /> Printed Decipher sets begin with [[Premiere Limited]] (December 1995); the full Decipher expansion list is on the [[Main Page]].

== After the license ==

''Main articles: [[Decipher after the Star Wars license]], [[Decipher and the Star Wars CCG Lucasfilm license]]''

Decipher lost the ''Star Wars'' license when its contract was not renewed; the license ended in December 2001. Company leadership publicly supported a Players' Committee and advocate structure so organized play and later virtual cards could continue.<ref name="wp-swccg" /><ref name="hist">[[History of the Players Committee]]</ref><ref name="lotr-decipher" /> After 2001 the game's stewardship passed to the community and the [[Players Committee]].<ref name="hist" />

== Decline ==

Decipher contracted over several years after license losses and underperforming launches. FanHQ and fan-club magazine efforts faded as social media grew. ''WARS'' and several youth CCGs struggled, RPG lines were cut, and staff reductions delayed late sets for its remaining licensed games. Physical product ended after ''Fight Klub'' (c. 2008), while decipher.com posted intermittent "coming back" messages for years afterward.<ref name="lotr-decipher" /><ref name="wp-decipher" />

=== Embezzlement ===

Former Decipher finance executive '''Rick Eddleman''', Holland's brother-in-law, pleaded guilty to embezzling more than US$1.5&nbsp;million from the company.<ref name="wp-decipher" /><ref name="pilot-plea">[https://web.archive.org/web/20090316043101/http://hamptonroads.com/node/501025 Norfolk man pleads guilty to embezzling more than $1.5m], ''The Virginian-Pilot'' (Internet Archive)</ref> In 2009 he was sentenced to about six years in prison.<ref name="pilot-sentence">[https://web.archive.org/web/20121002195010/http://hamptonroads.com/2009/07/game-company-embezzler-gets-6-years-must-repay-910000 Game company embezzlement was betrayal to family], ''The Virginian-Pilot'' (Internet Archive)</ref> A civil settlement came to about US$8.9&nbsp;million.<ref name="wp-decipher" /> According to documents Holland posted online, losses over Eddleman's 1990s–2001 tenure were about US$9&nbsp;million.<ref name="lotr-decipher" /><ref name="embezzle-site">[https://web.archive.org/web/20091005031807/http://www.embezzlementfromdecipher.com/ EmbezzlementFromDecipher.com], archived overview hosted by Holland (Internet Archive)</ref>
